key_insight: Occupations with higher AI exposure tend to have less dull, dirty, and dangerous work, but accounting for occupational characteristics weakens this association.
engineering_relevance: Use occupational AI exposure to identify contrasting research settings, not as proof that an AI intervention will relieve undesirable work.
method: Assess working conditions using 21 O*NET items across 754 US occupations.
Compare LLM exposure and AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE) using equal occupation and employment weights.
Adjust for physical demands, education, training, experience, and wages; separate repetition from restricted discretion.
evidence_signal: Adjusted confidence intervals for the composite association include zero for LLM exposure but remain below zero for AIOE.
watch_item: Exposure estimates do not establish workers’ desire for automation or realized relief; both require worker-preference and intervention evidence.
paper_title: Dull, Dirty, Dangerous? Working Conditions and the Limits of Occupational AI Exposure
